relations.evidence: If you change the sync function to revoke a user's access to a document, the access only takes effect once you save a new revision to that document on Sync Gateway. Running a resync operation does not revoke access to that document.

notable_absence.finding: The page warns about a hazard (running resync on more than one node in non-persistent-configuration mode: 'Starting resync on more than 1 node results in multiple instances running, with undefined system behavior') but never states a cleanup procedure to run if that hazard occurs - no requiresExplicitCleanupOnFailure shape, just a prevention warning. Nor does resync bypass any 'normal schedule' - it has no automatic/scheduled counterpart to pre-empt, unlike the eventing/xdcr scheduled-task 'run now' shape that triggersImmediateExecutionOf was minted for elsewhere in the registry - so that predicate does not apply here either.

cross_component_finding: The database.sync/Sync Function reference material (server-side JS, documented in access-control/) and this manage/ page describe two faces of the same object: what the Sync Function computes (access-control/sync-function.md) versus what happens when you change it after documents already exist (this page). Round 3's access-control extraction never anticipated 'what if the sync function changes after the fact' - it documented the function's write-time behavior only. This is the clearest piece of evidence in this batch that manage/ needed genuinely new vocabulary (sgw:resync-operation itself) even though it could reuse existing access-control concepts (sgw:sync-function, the require*Cmd family, sgw:channel-access-revocation) as the objects/subjects of its NEW relations - a middle case between round 26's Server node-lifecycle finding (zero precedent anywhere) and a hypothetical case where access-control vocabulary alone would have sufficed.
